name: dsDNA µg to pmol Calculator
seoTitle: dsDNA µg to pmol Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Converting dsDNA from micrograms to picomoles needs the fragment length, nothing else. Free dsdna µg to pmol calculator: enter your values and get amount, mas
summary:
Converting dsDNA from micrograms to picomoles needs the fragment length, nothing else. It returns amount, mass, mass and number of molecules, and the panel shows all of them at once.

A ligation, a sequencing reaction and a self-made standard all ask for a molar amount, while the bench gives you nanograms on a spectrophotometer — this does the arithmetic both ways at the exact length of your fragment. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the dsDNA µg to pmol
sections.html:
pmol = mass (µg) × 10⁶ ÷ (660 × length in bp). Molecules = mass (g) ÷ (660 × length) × 6.022 × 10²³

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
660average molar mass of one base pairg/mol
Nfragment lengthbp
pmolpicomole, 10⁻¹² molmol

sections.title: How do I use the dsDNA µg to pmol?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the length of the double-stranded molecule in base pairs.
  2. Type the mass in micrograms, or the amount in picomoles — whichever you know.
  3. The other value is solved for you, together with the molecule count.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: fragment length of 1,000 bp.

Substituting them into the formula gives amount of 1.52 pmol, mass of 1 µg, mass of 1,000 ng, number of molecules of 912,445,569,697.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
under 100 bpOligo-likeuse the single-strand or oligo converters instead
100 – 5 000 bpTypical fragmentthe 660 g/mol per bp average is accurate to a few percent
above 10 000 bpLarge moleculepipetting error dominates the conversion

  • 660 g/mol per base pair is the sodium salt average at 50% GC. At 70% GC the true figure is closer to 640, a 3% difference that matters only for quantitative work.

  • A 1 000 bp fragment weighs 660 kDa, so 1 µg is about 1.5 pmol — the number worth remembering at the bench.

  • Ligations are usually set up at a 1:3 vector-to-insert molar ratio rather than equal mass, which is exactly what this conversion gives you.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Using the single-stranded constant (330 g/mol per nucleotide) for a duplex, which halves the answer.
  • Forgetting that the length must be the whole molecule, not the insert.
  • Rounding a 20 ng measurement to 1 µg of 'measured' DNA.

faq.q: How many pmol is 100 ng of a 1 kb dsDNA?

faq.a: It is the average of the four base pairs' sodium salts, weighted for equal base composition.

faq.q: Can I use this for ssDNA?
faq.a: No — use 330 g/mol per nucleotide for single-stranded DNA or RNA.

faq.q: What does the dsDNA µg to pmol actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns amount, mass, mass and number of molecules. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
